utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-69-PT, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning. The attorneys representing the Prosecution here this morning are myself, Dermot Groome, David Re, and Melissa Pack. We are assisted today by Skye Winner and Rachel Friedman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Knoops, lead counsel in the case of Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Knoops. And for Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I am Zoran Jovanovic, attorney from Belgrade, representing Franko Simatovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. This is an application by the two accused, Franko Simatovic and Jovica Stanisic, for provisional release. The Chamber decided to hear the matters separately. The two accused are present, because, as has been indicated by the order which was issued, we will hear the government minister and representative, one after the other so that they will not have to give evidence twice. When the minister and the government representative have finished their evidence, we'll proceed with the Simatovic application. When that application is finished, we'll have a short Status Conference, and at the end of that hearing, we'll move on to the application by the accused Stanisic. Let me make two rulings before we proceed. First, in relation to the Defence, the Chamber decided that Defence could have a week in which to cross-examine the two Prosecution investigators, and I wanted to find out from the Defence whether they will choose to take that further time or whether they will proceed with cross-examination today. Can I hear first from Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, after your ruling, when you agreed to the interview with the investigator, in agreement with my learned friend Mr. Knoops, we decided to carry out the cross-examination immediately. But Mr. Knoops will present his remarks with respect to the cross-examination of these two witnesses, and I will join him in that. There's just one further point I wish to make in that context. We have just received a confidential memorandum from the Prosecution with a list of all the evidence and expert reports that have been disclosed so far. However, under number 2, a document is exhibited, that is, a newspaper article that the Defence was not disclosed, nor was it mentioned in any filing of the Prosecution. Even in the last filing, suggesting the cross-examination of these witnesses, this article was never mentioned. So it is not clear to us what the context is, and the Defence has not had a chance to respond to this. And the Defence could certainly respond to the facts contained in that article. So I would like the Prosecution to provide some clarification on this point, if possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the Chamber is also aware of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are not aware of it, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've simply assembled the documents that I may question some of the Defence witnesses with and I've just assembled them in the same binder. At the end of the hearing today I may be requesting that some of them be accepted into evidence, but it is a document that I do wish to -- or a newspaper article which I do wish to inquire to the government witnesses are they aware of this and ask them questions about it. I'm not aware that I have any disclosure obligation regarding questions I'm going to ask their witnesses and it's simply a copy of a newspaper article that appeared recently in the Belgrade press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We'll deal with that when we come to it. Mr. Knoops, you had some remarks to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Like my learned friend Mr. Jovanovic expressed, we will not request the Trial Chamber to adjourn for a week for potential cross-examination of the two OTP investigators. We, though, like to stress again our objection against the hearing of the two investigators, because we believe that their statements do not comply with the criteria as set forth by the Appeals Chamber in the Kordic case, in the judgement of 21 July 2000, where the Appeals Chamber has set forth six specific circumstances under which hearsay evidence can be admitted into the proceedings. And we also respectfully draw your attention to the ruling of your Trial Chamber in the Milosevic case, where the OTP investigator Mr. Kelly was refused to take the stand by the Trial Chamber based on these same criteria. So therefore, we respectfully ask Your Honours to eventually reconsider your decision, but for the record, we would like to stress our objection against the hearing of the two OTP investigators. Aside from the time-frame, we think -- we believe strongly that their statements do not comply, in short, with the Appeals Chamber's criteria. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should say that I think there's a clear distinction between this case and that of Mr. Kelly, who was a summarising witness. The Chamber doesn't see the two OTP investigators as summarising witnesses. The other ruling which I wish to make was in relation to an application by the Prosecutor to have the transcript of Dr. Smalc from another trial admitted under Rule 92 bis (D). This application is refused. It is clearly out of time. Mr. Groome, I should say in relation to the witness Dr. Boomgaard, the Chamber will allow him to give evidence, and at the end of the hearing we will try to work out an appropriate time to hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have spoken to him this morning and we will have the most current information regarding his availability when the Chamber wishes to discuss that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. May we then begin hearing submissions, opening submissions on behalf of the accused Franko Simatovic. Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. First of all, could we deal with the application for provisional release which has been marked as confidential, because there are quotations from the disclosed material, material disclosed by the Prosecution, which was disclosed to the Defence as confidential. And that is the only reason, so we can consider this to be partially confidential, that is, only with regard to parts of the transcript that were disclosed to the Defence as being confidential, and the mention of a particular witness in that filing. As regards all the other submissions, there's no reason for this to be confidential, nor for us to consider or hear this application in closed session. Therefore, the Defence of Mr. Simatovic would like this to be made in public hearing; if the Prosecution agrees, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection but for tab 5 of the exhibits that the Prosecution intends to use, and that's an affidavit of Investigator O'Donnell does contain some information which might compromise current OTP operations. I would ask that reference to that be taken in closed session and that it be placed under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You have heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. May I add something? Regarding the closed session during the hearing of this witness, should I mention that straight away or when we come to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can mention it when we come to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting, but if I could just point out that the transcript at 9:44:33 records Mr. Knoops as speaking when it was Mr. Jovanovic was speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That amendment will be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, the Defence for the accused Franko Simatovic, in its application for provisional release, as well as through responses to the filings of the Prosecution, has provided arguments in favour of the position that the conditions provided for under Rule 65 have been met. The Defence believes that on the basis of the arguments presented to the Trial Chamber, it can be confident that the accused will appear and that his provisional release will not put at risk any witness or victim. Also, as a necessary element of the application for provisional release, guarantees have also been provided by the government of the Republic of Serbia and the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro. The guarantees of the Republic of Serbia have been filed in the form of two conclusions; first, a conclusion of the previous government and a conclusion of the current government of the Republic of Serbia. And Mr. Stojkovic is the minister of justice in that government, who we will be hearing today. And Mr. Caric will also be present as a representative of the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro. With regard to the first condition, that is, whether Franko Simatovic will appear for trial: Allow me to say that, as a relevant and most important fact stressed by the Defence, and why we feel that we can assure the Trial Chamber that the accused will appear for trial is his personal attitude towards the Tribunal. That attitude has been demonstrated by the accused Franko Simatovic on several occasions, starting from cooperation with the Prosecution, which dates back to the beginning of 2002. There was an interview that went on for about 30 hours, and Mr. Franko Simatovic stated clearly on that occasion that he considers this Tribunal to be a Tribunal of his country as well, in view of its membership in the United Nations. On that occasion, and later on - and this is to be found in my submissions - he repeated this position of his, that is, that he would cooperate with this Tribunal in every shape and form; and perhaps most importantly, he fully recognises the jurisdiction of this Tribunal in establishing his possible guilt. And at the end of this interview that he granted to my learned friends from the Prosecution, after being presented with the suspicions and with the charges made against him - even after that - he said that he considered this Tribunal to be a Tribunal of his country as well and that he will respond to summons, considering this to be his duty. This is the first point which can serve as assurances that the accused will appear for trial. Regardless of the personal attitude of the accused which I have already described, it is essential for the state where the accused would be staying if he were to be provisionally released has to make its position clear and it has done so, to the effect that it will comply with all the obligations that may be imposed on the state by this Tribunal should the accused be provisionally released. In view of the position of the Defence, as presented with regard to the personal attitude of the accused towards the Tribunal, the Defence feels that should the accused Franko Simatovic be provisionally released and when being summoned to trial, the assistance of the state would not be necessary, in fact. It would only be necessary to the extent of issuing him with a passport which he is not in the possession of just now. When we come to guarantees, the Prosecution's practice so far, and in this case too, has linked guarantees to the level of cooperation of the state with the Tribunal. That is the Republic of Serbia and the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro. Any lack of cooperation of this kind compromises such guarantees. The Defence is of the opinion, in view of the established practice of the Tribunal, that in each individual application for provisional release, the facts need to be established which are relevant to that case and to those charges. We feel that guarantees should not necessarily be derived out of the context of other elements typical for that particular case, and they should not be linked exclusively to the general level of cooperation of a particular state -- that is, the view that a certain state is not cooperating fully because it hasn't fulfilled all its obligations. I think this should be put in more concrete form and it should be stated that the guarantees provided by the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro as well as the union of the two have always functioned. All persons that have been provisionally released so far did appear before the Tribunal when summoned. While those persons were on provisional release, the state authorities fully complied with all their obligations, with all their duties such as supervision of the accused, regular reporting to the Tribunal about their movements, and so on. Therefore, in the practice of this Court so far, the Republic of Serbia has never once failed in fulfilling its obligations in any -- by any individual act, and that is why we feel that it would be a simplified attitude to link this to the fact that a state cannot or will not surrender a fugitive. This should not be linked to the application of a particular suspect for provisional release. Attached to my application for provisional release, I have attached an article from New York Times, but for other reasons, but I will mention it now, since the Prosecution is asking the Trial Chamber to admit into evidence the letter of the president of the Tribunal, Mr. Theodor Meron. And his position is that Serbia and Montenegro are not cooperating at present. However, this text, dating back from July last year - actually, ten months ago - Judge Meron said that a new spirit of cooperation is coming from Belgrade and that one has to see how many people, high-ranking people had been arrested and surrendered to the Tribunal. This was stated ten months ago. I'm just trying to say that this cooperation with respect to guarantees may be variable. The position is not that Serbia and Montenegro are definitely not cooperating with the Tribunal. The Minister of Justice, Mr. Zoran Stojkovic, and the representative of the union will have an opportunity to state clearly what the plans are of that state union with respect to cooperation with the Tribunal. It is a fact that the president of the Tribunal at this point in time feels that Serbia and Montenegro are not cooperating, but we will hear from the representatives of that union what their views are. However, we feel that this shouldn't be viewed in simplified terms. One cannot say there's no cooperation or there is cooperation. It is a more complex matter than that. And I will use a similar method as was used by my learned friend Mr. Groome in his response to the Defence application. He says that he has knowledge of a certain fact. And I would like to say the same, that I have certain knowledge which I'm sure the Prosecution shares; that is, knowledge with regard to an example of a country which, upon the invitation of the Prosecution to state whether it accepts the subpoenas of the Tribunal and subpoenas of the Trial Chamber, it answered loud and clear that it was contrary to its legal system and that it cannot comply with the requirements of this Tribunal. And it is interesting to note that that country considers this Tribunal to be an alien Tribunal. It is not under the jurisdiction of this Tribunal, but is a member of the United Nations, and it does delegate judges to this Court. This was not included in the Prosecution's report to the Tribunal's president. So it is their opinion that even though they have clearly stated that they would not accept subpoenas, they still consider them to be cooperating. I think such situations too should be taken into consideration when assessing the cooperation of the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro or the Republic of Serbia with the Tribunal. With respect to the other condition envisaged by Rule 65, and that is whether the accused will appear for trial, that is the Trial Chamber must be confident that he will not threaten in any way witnesses, victims or any other persons while on provisional release. In their response, the Prosecution says that the accused Franko Simatovic was employed in the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia; actually, the Defence explained that the state security at the time, the State Security Service, was one of two sectors of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and the Prosecutor interprets this as meaning that the accused has knowledge and information as to where Prosecution witnesses may be residing, that he might locate them and influence them. With regard to the relationship between the accused and the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia, the Defence has explained in its application and response. The accused was arrested without any grounds by that same Ministry of Defence, and I go back to the text of the New York Times, which I have submitted and which the Prosecution has considered as insignificant but not incorrect. That article also contains those facts. Therefore, Franko Simatovic was arrested without any reason, and judging by the assertions in this article, officials of the former Serbian government asked for assistance. I'll explain what this is all about. He was arrested on the 13th of March, and this indictment was confirmed on the 1st of May. When Franko Simatovic was interviewed by the investigating judge, he ruled detention beginning on the 13th of March. This was subsequently changed. So what this means is that he was arrested without any grounds, and then every effort was made to legalise this procedure. And when they failed to do so, then - according to Madam Carla Del Ponte - the officials of the former government asked her for her assistance, saying that they had no reason to keep in detention on remand the accused and could the Prosecution assist by indicting him, and of course arresting him. According to the words of my learned friend, Del Ponte, the investigation was expedited. At that moment, the OTP had no intention of raising an indictment because the investigation by that time had not been completed. However, at the request of officials of the Serbian government, the OTP simply expedited their investigation in order to accommodate officials of the Serbian government so that they could use this to justify this unwarranted detention. It is in this sense that the Defence believes that there was a third party that directly affected the time of detention itself. The raising of the indictment means that first there was an order for detention. And this was all done at a time when this proved very convenient for certain officials of the previous Serbian government and not the OTP. The beginning of Mr. Simatovic's detention chronologically follows his arrest in Belgrade and was directly affected by the third party. The Defence believes this is a violation of Article 16 of the Statute. As for the OTP's allegations in relation to the relevance of the allegations made against Mr. Simatovic possibly leading him not to appear before this Court, the Defence has stated on several occasions before that he is familiar with such suspicions. He was interviewed for a long time and was familiarised with the general nature of the OTP's investigation and was fully familiar with it even in relation to the time-frame that the indictment refers to, 1992 to 1995. It is actually quite a long time-frame. Towards the end of the interview, and later, he gave all these statements that I have referred to, and these indicate that he is willing to fully cooperate with the Tribunal. He was familiarised before with what potential witnesses would be, but none of those persons who later testified in the Milosevic case - and there was quite a number of such witnesses testifying in the Milosevic case who in one context or another also referred to this accused - none of those persons ever said that they were threatened or jeopardised by the accused Franko Simatovic. As for the weight of the accusations themselves, I believe it is a simple piece of demagoguery to state these as the reason why someone should not be provisionally released. It is clear that all the trials based on indictments raised before this Tribunal are in relation to very serious allegations against people who stand indicted. The United Nations resolution specifies that these are the most serious crimes possible, and the responsibility for these crimes is equally great. Now, in relation to indictments that have before been raised before this Tribunal -- follow the same criterion. It is perfectly clear that trials are being conducted before this Court for the most serious crimes possible, and the same applies to this case as to all the other cases before this Tribunal. Rule 65, however, provides for the possibility of provisional release, and this is a well-known procedure in the case-law of this Tribunal. As we know, a number of high-positioned persons who held political offices have been known to be provisionally released before this Tribunal and to appear for trial. Therefore, Your Honours, the Defence of the accused Franko Simatovic believes that all the conditions have been met as required by Rule 65, first through the personal attitude displayed by the accused Franko Simatovic in his statements, and as we know, these statements are relevant for this Tribunal. I would like to remind the Court of the arguments put forward by the OTP during the procedure for the provisional release of the accused Sainovic and Ojdanic. The OTP attempted to prove that there was no goodwill on the part of the accused to surrender themselves. However, the accused Franko Simatovic, in addition to his statements, the statements that he gave clearly displayed his willingness to cooperate with the Tribunal. Was he telling the truth? I believe the OTP does not have the jurisdiction to decide over that, and there should be a conclusion, a final conclusion, as to Mr. Simatovic collaborated or not, was he telling the truth or not. He was cooperating. Indeed he was, even without the assistance of state organs. It wasn't even necessary for the OTP to appeal for help to the state organs to get Mr. Simatovic's cooperation. He cooperated without any of the state bodies knowing about it. He cooperated before the law was even adopted on cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal that many people later referred to. Mr. Simatovic was not even familiar with that law. He sees himself in a direct relationship with this Tribunal, a personal relationship. On the basis of the guarantees that have been issued in relation to the motion for provisional release, all the conditions have been met as required by Rule 65. I pointed out that some degree of cooperation has been achieved, unfortunately, contrary to the Statute and the rules, with Serbian officials from the previous government and the OTP. I do not believe the Chamber should accept this. If the OTP agrees to have that kind of cooperation, I believe at least the Chamber should not approve this in its ruling. Therefore, I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to grant provisional release for the accused Mr. Franko Simatovic until the start of his trial. He will be staying in Yugoslavia. And please rest assured that he will answer any summons that may be sent to him from this Tribunal. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just say I allowed my learned colleague to complete his remarks, but I would be remiss if I did not point out at this point that I do take issue with his alleged quote of Ms. Carla Del Ponte. He has misquoted the Prosecutor and he's also mischaracterised the nature of her interaction with the Serbian government around the time that the accused Mr. Simatovic was arrested. He has suggested a quite serious allegation to the Chamber. I'm not -- I don't believe it's appropriate matter for provisional release. I would ask that if he believes that such an allegation is founded that he make a proper motion so that it can be dealt with in a more proper fashion than by innuendo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, your first witness. Do you want to reply to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may just briefly. I have just quoted an article, one paragraph of the article that I attached to my motion, and it is up to the OTP to respond to that. Please believe me that the Defence of Mr. Simatovic also found this quite strange. That's why I clearly stated this in my motion, to give the OTP a chance to respond. Just as Mr. Groome has responded. This was probably a misrepresentation, and the OTP was given a chance to say that it was. However, they themselves clearly stated they believed it irrelevant. Was this a misinterpretation on my part? Perhaps. Or perhaps the misinterpretation was contained in the original article. Had the OTP responded in a timely manner, the Defence would have been given a chance to call the author of the text himself or perhaps to make other sources available. But the OTP failed to speak about it, failed to address this issue. Even now, I can only say that I'm sorry if the OTP believes that I have acted in an unfair manner in any way whatsoever, but this is a fact. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We proceed now to the hearing of the witnesses. Mr. Simatovic, your first witness. You intend to call the minister, Minister Stojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... To both accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Jovanovic. Let the witness be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic and Mr. Groome, I just want to confirm that the government minister will be giving evidence and will be subject to cross-examination, will make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would expect that every witness that takes the witness chair would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's my expectation too, yes. Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I fully agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why is it taking so long for the witness to appear, Madam Registrar? Is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will check. I have no idea why it's taking so long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness will be here shortly, I'm advised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit. Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stojkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkovic. Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In accordance with Article 36 of the law on co-operation -- my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic will ask you some questions. Examined by Mr. Jovanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Stojkovic. My name is Zoran Jovanovic. I represent the accused Franko Simatovic before this Tribunal. Please state your name and your official position.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Zoran Stojkovic, minister of justice in the government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stojkovic. Mr. Stojkovic, the government of the Republic of Serbia, on the 6th of May, 2004, adopted a conclusion confirming the conclusion of the government of the Republic of Serbia in its previous establishment, providing the guarantees for cooperation of the Republic of Serbia with the International Criminal Tribunal in the case, in the eventuality of the provisional release of Franko Simatovic. Would you provide further clarification as to what these guarantees mean exactly and why these were provided for the accused Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: According to Article 36 on the law of the cooperation with this Tribunal, the Council of Ministers and the republican government envisaged a possibility that the Trial Chamber would grant provisional release for any of the accused and the Republic takes upon itself the obligation to provide certain guarantees in relation to the provisional release of these persons. There are a number of considerations that are included here. The person should stay in the country, as decided by the Council of Ministers. The person should report to the police every day. There should be reports on what has been achieved and whether the person is acting in accordance with orders of the Council of Ministers. Also, it should be made sure that this person will not be given a chance to run away or fail to attend any hearings requested by the Tribunal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stojkovic. When providing these guarantees, the conclusion was adopted at one of the government sessions, if I'm not mistaken. Please tell us: Was another matter taken into consideration? More specifically, who the guarantees are being issued in relation to, the specific person, and what was the reaction of the Council of Ministers and the Minister himself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies. The Council of Ministers had already adopted a decision to issue the guarantees in compliance with the decision made by the previous government. The new government found that there were no changes and that it was possible to confirm the guarantees in relation to Mr. Simatovic and Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically, Mr. Stojkovic, as you represent the government of the Republic of Serbia also, the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, is it willing and able to arrest Mr. Franko Simatovic should he fail to respond to any of the Tribunal's summons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: These are the guarantees that have been provided. He should report to the Ministry of the Interior on a daily basis and file a report to the government every month. In my opinion, it would be perfectly simple to arrest him at any given time should the necessity arise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkovic, in relation to previous cases before the new government was established, in which you are the minister of justice, the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro, did they function in relation to provisionally released persons? Did Serbia and Montenegro live up to its obligations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know. In relation to Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Strugar, it was Montenegro specifically, and Mr. Jokic too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkovic, what will the cooperation be like between the government of the Republic of Serbia and the International Criminal Tribunal? Is there an official position of the government of the Republic of Serbia, and how exactly does the Republic of Serbia see or view its obligations towards the International Criminal Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: As for the cooperation itself, I think this has been stated with perfect clarity. These are our obligations towards the Tribunal and we have to meet these. It would not be fair to go any further into this, as I am also about to speak to Mr. Meron and therefore I do not wish now to enter into any further detail of this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stojkovic. Mr. Franko Simatovic's Defence has no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Knoops:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stojkovic. I'm the Defence attorney of Mr. Stanisic. First of all, your remarks just put to the Trial Chamber, do they also count for the situation of Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the specific position of Mr. Stanisic, both the federal government and your government issued a guarantee for the secure of provisional release. Now, in the guarantee of the federal government, mention is made of the existence of humanitarian grounds for provisional release. My specific question for you is: Is your government able to supervise Mr. Stanisic's potential treatment in his home country, and if so, to which extent?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in relation to his health problems? I am not in a position to speak about that. You should ask medical experts about this. As for treatment, we have some institutions that are very good, and he had previously received treatment in those institutions. I don't think there should be any --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Government is able to enforce the conditions in case provisional release is allowed that Mr. Stanisic would attend trial.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: As I said before, even if there should be a problem we would be prepared to arrest him and to make sure that he would attend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to Yugoslav law, is it correct that Mr. Stanisic surrendered voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking me about something that's difficult to define. What was going on at a time when the situation in the country was very difficult. There was a state of emergency, and several measures could have been applied. Arrest was merely one of them. At the time the indictment was published, as far as I know, both Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic declared their willingness to immediately leave for The Hague and appear before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it in your view correct that at the time of the detention of Mr. Stanisic, no criminal charges were raised against him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the same applies to the situation today, with the exception of arrest. The OTP never put forward a request for investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question for the witness. Mr. Stojkovic, were you able to verify whether or not Mr. Stanisic is in the possession of a valid passport?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. This was not our obligation for the time being. This can be verified. It is down to the Ministry of the Interior to issue passports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groome. Cross-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stojkovic. My name is Dermot Groome and I'll be representing the Prosecutor at these proceedings this morning. I'd like to focus the limited time that you are here and pick up on one of the answers that you gave Mr. Jovanovic. In response to him asking you why it was or how it was that you would fulfil the obligation of returning Mr. Simatovic, if necessary, you said, and I'm quoting the English translation: "These are our obligations toward the Tribunal." Do you fully intend to recognise your obligations towards the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: With respect to this particular case, I have said that it was not only our obligation towards the Tribunal, but should there be any doubt as to the voluntary nature of Mr. Stanisic's response to summons from this Tribunal, he would be arrested and handed over to the Tribunal. I apologise if we misunderstand one another. What I was saying was that we would arrest him and make sure that he would come to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me then ask you: Arrest warrants had been lodged with your government with respect to an indictment against Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Pavkovic, Mr. Lukic. My question to you is: Are you aware that arrest warrants have been lodged with respect to these men?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there are quite a number of problems there. Since there has been a change in the government, a council for cooperation with the Tribunal has still not been appointed, and that is the council that has the responsibilities for future action. So we're still in an interim situation, because this body that is supposed to regulate cooperation with the Tribunal has still not been fully formed. But we are aware of the existence of these indictments and we will certainly act in accordance with our obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When did the new government come into being, Mr. Stojkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 4th of March, 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, it seems that you're saying that it is your intention on behalf of your government to guarantee here that the obligations towards the Tribunal will be fulfilled except if problems arise, such as the one you've just described here. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the government has so far acted accordingly, at least as far as I know. There was no request from this Tribunal that was not fulfilled in terms of the disclosure of documents, the surrender of a number of people voluntarily. So percentage-wise, the largest number of detainees here in The Hague come from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I won't go into the details of cooperation with respect to documents with you. I would refocus your attention on the fact that there are a number of publicly indicted people for which arrest warrants have been lodged, and in fact in this past December of 2003, both Mr. Lukic and Mr. Pavkovic both even ran for general election. Is that not true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: That is certainly true, but I'm trying to explain that obligations towards the Hague Tribunal is in the hands of the council for cooperation which currently doesn't exist. And these persons took part in the elections earlier on, before the new government came into power. That is what I was trying to explain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can I take from your answer that you are recognising that cooperation with respect to executing search warrants has been incomplete in the past, but that you are pledging here today that once this council is operating, that we can expect full compliance? Is that what you're conveying to us this morning?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The government has already issued an official declaration that it will cooperate, that it considers it not only a question of cooperation but its duty and obligation towards the Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkovic, when will this council be established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid this is something that doesn't depend on the government of the Republic of Serbia. It is at the level of the Union, and they have to decide about this and appoint members to the council. I'm trying to explain the procedure. The council is the one that receives indictments and passes on to -- then to the courts. The court then addresses itself to the Ministry of the Interior for the arrest and then the proceedings are started in motion with respect to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, so then your guarantee that you are offering here today, it's conditioned upon something that's outside of your control, namely, that a council will be formed for cooperation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The council existed, but now that the government has changed, the composition of various bodies is changing, and all these bodies have not fully been formed yet. All I am saying now is that the government has issued an official statement saying that it will cooperate with the Hague Tribunal. I was just trying to explain, because you asked me something that is not within the competence of republican authorities but of the federal authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But would you agree that until that council has taken effect, that your guarantee that you offer here today is unenforceable?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This part is something that we can enforce. The first stage has been completed. The suspects have been surrendered to the Tribunal. Should they be released, then it is our obligation - the Ministry of the Interior - to make sure that he does respond to summons, and should the person fail to do so, we would arrest him and surrender him to the Tribunal under escort. So the situation is not identical in the two cases. It's the same -- the same applies as with Mrs. Plavsic. When she was provisionally released, the procedure of surrender to the Tribunal was fully complied with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that there's a difference. Can you explain to us: How is an arrest warrant for an Initial Appearance different from somebody appearing before the Court being provisionally released and being required but failing to return a second time? What is so different about those two situations, that we should accept a guarantee to return a provisionally released person but not a person who has been -- an arrest warrant has been executed or issued for?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In these two cases, the persons have already received the indictments during regular proceedings. They are in the Hague Tribunal. Should they be provisionally released, they would be brought back under our supervision. The council for cooperation with the Hague Tribunal has still not given the necessary instructions for the republican authorities to be able to react. That is the difference. So the procedure has not even started. However, in this case, it has, and the republican authorities take upon themselves the obligation to fully carry out the whole procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the distinction, but I'm going to move on to a second area. Part of the Chamber's consideration will be the impact on witnesses that provisional release of these men would have. In that vein, I'm sure you're aware that recently, in April, during a trial in Belgrade, a number of further Red Berets wearing their insignias and identifying shirts appeared in the court. This act was considered by some in your government as an act of intimidation, an act of intimidation not only to witnesses but to the court personnel itself. Are you aware that the indictment here alleges that both Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic were superiors of members of the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The case you are referring to is something I'm familiar with. As far as I know, after verification, not one of those persons was actually a member of the Red Berets. The man who gave an interview and provoked attention from the public proved never to have been a member of the Red Berets. And the young man who wore those T-shirts attending training but were never admitted. So they were not members of the Red Berets. But I agree that this caused some disturbance. However, all the witnesses were interrogated in the course of those proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's your evidence here today that these people were mere supporters of the Red Berets, not actual members of the Red Berets. Would that be an accurate accounting of what you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jovanovic. Mr. Stojkovic, Mr. Jovanovic is on his feet. Let us hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for giving me the floor. We've just come to the problem that I mentioned at the beginning. Mr. Groome is presenting certain facts here and endeavouring to extract an answer. After the text we have received here, there are a number of other articles denying the membership of those persons in the Red Berets. The Zandarmerija issued an announcement stating that they were never members of that unit, that the T-shirts that they were wearing were not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, let me stop you. You will have an opportunity for re-examine the witness. Those are matters that you can raise then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. What I said was based on facts. The person who granted an interview was taken into custody and the judge has started proceedings on charges of false reporting, and they were proven not to have been members, and this particular individual for who knows what reasons granted such an interview. So he's being taken to court for spreading falsehoods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkovic, accepting the facts as you have relayed them to us, would you not agree that for witnesses that may be inclined to cooperate with the Tribunal in this particular case currently living in Serbia and Montenegro, that such a public display of support for the Red Berets, and by virtue of their association with that organisation, the two accused here, would you not agree that their release provisionally would serve as a further intimidation or further frightening of witnesses inclined to come forward and testify about what they know about this organisation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is an opinion that I couldn't respond to. All I could give would be an opinion, and I'd rather talk about facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, let's move on. I think that issue has been sufficiently ventilated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question to you is: You know who Milorad Lukovic, "Legija", is, do you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Last week he turned himself in voluntarily to the Serb authorities, did he not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there's no question about whether or not he is a former member of the Red Berets, is there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member of the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today, Mr. Stojkovic, was Legija provisionally released in your country or is it not true that he is detained in your country at this present time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he's in detention, and he should make an initial appearance in court today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still have obligatory detention for the most serious crimes and this is something that we shall have to adjust to the convention. But we have this provision regarding detention. There's no possibility of having him released unless the court may pass such a decision. He is now within the jurisdiction of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, any re-examination? Briefly. I should say that we did set a timetable with specific times, and we are beyond it now. So we need to move ahead quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honours, in connection with this last question put by Mr. Groome to the witness. Re-examined by Mr. Jovanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of what is Mr. Lukic accused?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: For the murder of former Prime Minister Djindjic and for some other ten acts of murder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He may apply for release?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Any accused may do so, and it is up to the Court to make a ruling about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stojkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkovic, that concludes your evidence and you may now go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your next witness, Mr. Jovanovic and Mr. Knoops, is that Mr. Caric?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Caric, as a representative of the State Union of the Republics of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let him be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will he be examined as a witness or just make a statement as a representative of government?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that he will make a statement as a representative of the authorities, as the republican Minister of Justice has already presented his views regarding the possible actions of the Republic to which the accused may be released. The conclusion or the guarantees issued by the State Union are based on the conclusion of the republican authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, will you want to cross-examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He will then have to make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting, maybe we could make some productive use of the time. It occurred to me that in order to save time, if it pleases the Court, the Prosecution would be willing to tender the exhibit under 89(F), avoid having the investigators detail that. I leave it to the Court to decide whether it's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the accused Mr. Stanisic would like to make a short tour to the bathroom, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps -- should we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us take the 20-minute break now. We're adjourned. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Caric to be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit. Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I spoke to Mr. Caric, and he told me that he is here in the capacity of a representative of the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro and that he has not been authorised to answer any other questions except to confirm that guarantees have been issued by the Council of Ministers of the State Union. So I have no questions for Mr. Caric except to ask him whether he can confirm that the Council of Ministers of the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro has issued guarantees with respect to the accused Franko Simatovic. Has the State Union assumed the obligations indicated in the document that has been provided to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you answer the question, let me clarify what you're saying. You're saying that Mr. Caric is here to speak to one issue, and one issue only: That is, the issuance of the guarantee. And he has not been authorised to address any other issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That is exactly what I have been told. But perhaps Mr. Caric can tell you. I can ask Mr. Caric the question that I have mentioned: Can he confirm that the procedure has been carried out, and that the state Council of Ministers has issued such guarantees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Chamber will consult. Because the issue, it seems, is whether Mr. Caric will be subject to cross-examination. Mr. Groome has indicated that he wants to cross-examine him. There is a practice in proceedings of this kind for representatives to make statements as to the issuance of the guarantees. That's not usually done from the witness box. I'll consult with my colleagues on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Caric, I've heard what has been said by Mr. Jovanovic. You say you're only here to speak to the issuance of the guarantees. Would you be prepared to answer questions relating only to the issuance of the guarantees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just want to say two things in Serbian language as a clarification. [Interpretation] First of all, I'm here as a representative of the embassy, which means a representative of Serbia and Montenegro, of the diplomatic mission of Serbia and Montenegro in The Hague. I should come here to confirm the guarantees issued by Mr. Stojkovic. I was meant just to be present. I have no mandate to say anything further regarding the guarantees and their issuance. That is the first point I wish to make. And secondly, with your permission, I can hand over the original copy of the conclusions of the government of Serbia with respect to Mr. Franko Simatovic. By your leave, I can hand this over to the Trial Chamber. We have already sent copies through diplomatic mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber's decision is that you will make the statement, which is usual in these proceedings, without any questions being asked. Go ahead with your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just repeat: As I don't have the authority to make any statement, I fully abide by what has been said by Minister Stojkovic; and with your permission, I should like to hand over the original of the government conclusions confirming guarantees for Mr. Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please hand them over. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of the decisions that this Chamber will have to reach is how reliable such guarantees are. May I make the following suggestion, that we ask Mr. Caric to -- at a break, contact his government and see, is he authorised to answer questions about the guarantee, and so he can inquire about its reliability and we can move on to the next witnesses. And perhaps later in the day Mr. Caric will have obtained such authorisation and we can properly inquire about just how reliable this guarantee is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Caric has been quite clear as to the instructions that he has and what he's authorised to say. It's not the Court's view that the matter should be taken any further. Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Caric, in his statement, in fact confirmed the guarantees provided by the Republic of Serbia. Maybe he can tell us whether he can confirm the existence of the document entitled "Guarantees of the Council of Ministers of the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro." Can he confirm that such guarantees have been issued as a document by the Council of Ministers of the State Union?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does your position confirm that? You may sit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Minister Stojkovic has explained everything with respect to the guarantees, so I don't see why the reliability of those guarantees would be called in question. He was the authorised representative to confirm those guarantees, and all I can do is to confirm the explanations that he gave. And I can say that earlier those guarantees were in some cases elaborated by a representative of the embassy, sometimes by an official coming from our country. Mr. Stojkovic was authorised to explain the guarantees. He has done so fully, and all I can do is confirm everything that he has said. And if I were to say anything else, that would go beyond my authority. So I don't see why those guarantees would be called in question, as he has explained them, and since the Council of Ministers has issued guarantees. So I don't see that anything can be in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Caric. The document has been passed over to the Registrar, has it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It has, Your Honour, but it has to be translated in English language. It will be filed today and translated accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Caric. That concludes your statement. You may leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Do you wish to -- yes, well, the Defence has a question for the witness whether Mr. Caric has the same declaration to be issued, to be given in case of Mr. Stanisic. Because he only mentioned Mr. Simatovic. So my question for the witness is: Is he in a position to give a statement with respect to the guarantees, specifically in the case of Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as Minister Stojkovic has explained, the guarantees of the government of Serbia have been issued by both accused in this Tribunal, so I have nothing more to add to what the minister has already stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They apply to both accused. Thank you very much. You may leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, we will admit the statements under 89(F). I'm referring, of course, to the statements of the two investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will adjust my examination accordingly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: My full name is Bernard O'Donnell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to expedite matters we're going to take your evidence primarily in written form. I'd ask that a number be assigned to the binder of exhibits which the Prosecution has distributed earlier this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be numbered PT1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you ask you to take a look at tab 5 from that and ask you: Is that an affidavit authored by yourself and signed today?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If the usher would be so kind as to bring the document to Mr. O'Donnell.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. That is a document that I prepared and signed today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does that document summarise what information you have with respect to information that was provided to the government of Serbia and Montenegro and what if any action they took on that information?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, it does, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir I'd now ask you to take a look at tab 6 of PT1. I'd ask you the same question. Is that a document that you authored and signed?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It's a document dated the 5th of May. It's a document that I authored and signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does that document summarise your assessment of an interview that you conducted with Mr. Stanisic some time ago?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you affirm, now that you've been sworn under oath, that the information contained in both of these documents is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I tender both of those under 89(F).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. They're admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome the statement signed today, we received it today?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If Your Honour will recall, it was forecast in the last application. Mr. O'Donnell was away on mission. The contents of that was forecast in our application last week and it was provided this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How do you expect the Defence can cross-examine upon the document which they received just today?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was relying and was not opposing the Chamber's decision that they would have the opportunity to delay Mr. O'Donnell's cross-examination for one week. It seemed a perfectly fair decision by the Chamber, and they have stated, though, here in Court that they are prepared to cross-examine. If they should change their mind, Mr. O'Donnell is here, is available to be cross-examined when they feel they are ready. I do take note of Your Honour's observation that it is very short time. I would also point out that it's approximately a page and a half, though, of material, so it may very well be that they do feel equipped to examine him today. Your Honour, I forgot to mention I would ask tab 5 be under seal, if it takes place today; that it be done in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be so. Mr. Jovanovic, do you wish to revisit your decision to proceed with cross-examination today?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The Defence did not have a chance to inspect this statement. The first statement was given to the Defence team on Thursday afternoon, and we expressed our disapproval. In relation to that one, however, the Defence of Mr. Simatovic would not have any questions. The contents of that statement relate to the interview with Mr. Stanisic. However, in the statement that was disclosed to us today, there is reference to Mr. Simatovic also. Regardless of that, I will cross-examine today on this basis. However, I oppose the introduction of this statement and the questioning of this witness in relation to anything stated in this statement. We believe it is simply too late for that. We oppose the examination of the witness whose statements were delivered on Thursday afternoon. It was in the interest of justice that you ruled that all the interviewed persons be heard, but I believe this represents a misuse of your ruling. It was in the interest of justice that the Chamber has decided to hear all the persons that were interviewed, but the OTP is using that now to introduce new evidence just before the start of the trial. I believe this is simply unjust. I propose that we cross-examine witness Tore Soldal, but I would like to move that the OTP not be allowed to tender anything contained in today's statement into evidence, the statement marked tab 6 in the list provided by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me make it clear again. The issue of lateness and of possible embarrassment to the Defence is to be addressed by giving you the opportunity to delay your cross-examination. If you choose to proceed with it, that's entirely a matter for you. The Chamber, as it said before, is perfectly prepared to offer you a week in which to prepare for cross-examination. The Chamber is admitting the statements, and as I said, and I repeat, the issue of late service is to be addressed by granting you an opportunity to delay your cross-examination if you so wish. I understand that you wish to proceed in relation to one statement. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour. Thank you for offering the Defence a possibility to defer our cross-examination. However, the Defence team wishes to expedite proceedings, and we shall proceed with our cross-examination of the witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed. Yes. Cross-examined by Mr. Jovanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Donnell, based on the fact that Generals Lukic, Pavkovic, Djordjevic, and Lazarevic were not arrested in Serbia, is it your conclusion that there would be any danger to the carrying out of the proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal in relation to the accused Mr. Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Firstly, I don't quite understand your question. If it relates to the appropriateness of conducting proceedings, I'm not qualified to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't mean the appropriateness of conducting proceedings, but all the measures that need to be taken for proceedings to be carried out. More specifically, Mr. Simatovic appearing before the Court and his potential influence on the witnesses. Do you have a conclusion that you based on what you said in the statement to the effect that the generals are no longer at large pursuant to a request by the Tribunal, as well as the fact that some of them have been giving interviews to the press, specifically the references to these persons that you mentioned. Is it therefore your conclusion that Franko Simatovic for that very reason would fail to appear before the Court or that he would attempt to influence witnesses, put at risk victims, or rather, persons?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, the persons mentioned in the affidavit have been indicted and three of those persons are publicly at large. I also mentioned that several people indicted publicly by the Tribunal remain at large and information has been provided to authorities in Serbia and Montenegro. In fact, of those persons publicly indicted, the 20, 16 of those persons, according to information we have, remain in that territory. Therefore, I believe that it is a factor in relation to the matter being discussed; that is, the release of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic and undertakings given by local authorities when 16 of the 20 people publicly indicted, according to information we have at the Office of the Prosecutor, remain at large. Information has been passed to authorities in Serbia and Montenegro in relation to their locations within Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is your opinion, as an OTP investigator, that the accused Franko Simatovic would not appear before the Court again, based on these arguments that you've just put forward.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the question going more towards whether or not -- whether -- if Mr. Simatovic did not come voluntarily, whether action would be taken, given the fact that information has been given on other indictees and not acted upon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honours, my apologies. I believe the witness has misinterpreted my question. My question was: Is it his personal position or opinion that Simatovic would fail to respond to another summons by the Tribunal, based on the fact that the Generals Pavkovic, Lukic, and Lazarevic have not been arrested and are currently on the territory of the Republic of Serbia, at large, as well as other persons who have not received the indictment? Is that the position of this OTP investigator, that Mr. Simatovic would not show up in Court, based on this information?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I see that as being two separate factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to cross-examine the witness in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Private session, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect to the expert witnesses, Dr. Tarabar and Dr. Offermans, that will be no problem. The only thing is I have just learned from the case manager that your expert witness, the Minister of Health, will leave tomorrow -- today, later today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If it's of assistance to the Chamber, Mr. Soldal is available tomorrow, whenever the Court wishes to reschedule him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 1 (Redacted) 2 (Redacted) 3 (Redacted) 4 (Redacted) 5 (Redacted) 6 (Redacted) 7 (Redacted) 8 (Redacted) 9 (Redacted) 10 (Redacted) 11 (Redacted) 12 (Redacted) 13 (Redacted) 14 (Redacted) 15 (Redacted) 16 (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal to be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Groome. Examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: State your name, please.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Tore Soldal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long have you been an investigator in the Office of the Prosecutor here at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Around seven years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal, in order to expedite matters, I'm going to take much of your testimony in writing. I'm going to show you what is Exhibit PT 7, and ask you: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance with that, I'd appreciate it. Is that a document that you authored and signed?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does that document summarise your experience and your views with respect to the effect or the impact that the release of Mr. Simatovic and Mr. Stanisic would have on witnesses or potential witnesses in this case?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you now to take a look at tab 8 of that same Exhibit, PT1. Can you tell us what that document is?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: It's a declaration signed by me. It's about the interview I conducted with Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does that document contain your assessment of the value or of the contents of the information that Mr. Simatovic provided to you during that interview?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do both of those documents contain your signature?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that you have been sworn, do you affirm that the information contained in those documents is truthful and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender those exhibits, tab 7 and tab 8 of PT1 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, they're admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Jovanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Soldal, tell me, please: How did the interview with Mr. Simatovic take place? Or to be more specific, did you establish contact with am him yourself, directly, or through any state organ?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: It was one of my colleagues that established the contact with Mr. Simatovic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the official authorities of the Republic of Serbia had no part in it?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Soldal, do you remember whether the law on cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal had been passed at the time by the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it hadn't been passed at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal, in your statement, you said that the interview was held in a friendly atmosphere. Could you elaborate a little, and could you also tell us where it took place and a few words to elaborate the actual interview.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Most of the interview took place in the apartment of Mr. Simatovic. The last part was in the apartment of one of his lawyers. The interview was done in a very friendly atmosphere. Mr. Simatovic brought food, coffee, drinks, was friendly. No problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal, do you remember that Franko Simatovic suggested that the interview take place in his apartment, and when he did so, did he mention his doubts about security? Did he mention that he or members of his family were at some sort of risk?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: I can't remember that now. It may have happened, but the first meetings with him was done by -- one of my colleagues, Vladimir Dzuro. But it also may have happened during the interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal, so you do allow for the possibility that your colleagues may have some additional information regarding this event?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: May have. It's quite a long time since, but they may have some additional information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal, do you know what Mr. Simatovic said when he reached the Detention Unit in The Hague, when he was interviewed again? Do you perhaps recollect that he then mentioned that he was fearful for his family members?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Absolutely. He feared what could happen to his sons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
