utterances.text: May I infer from that that he himself considered himself to be at risk, in a sense, both in Belgrade and later when he came here he feared for the members of his family, and he told you that? Thank you. Mr. Soldal, you are certainly familiar with the indictment, which is effective after the preliminary objections were filed. Are you aware of the dates mentioned here for various crimes? Do you remember when the crimes listed in SAO Krajina were committed in Vukovar, the autonomous region of Baranja and Western Srem, Bijeljina, Bosanski Samac? I assume you will that those were the results of your own investigations. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: I am not -- I do not remember all the dates of all the crimes on the top of my head. I've only been involved in a few of the crime bases. But approximately I know when the different crimes in the indictment are supposed to happen, take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that, with the exception of Sanski Most and another crime in Mrkonjic grad, in all other cases, and this ends with paragraph 57, that they all refer to 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal, what was Franko Simatovic's position in 1991/1992 in the Ministry of Internal Affairs, or rather, what did your investigation show?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Objection as to relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jovanovic. What's the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this? It seems more like a matter for trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, Your Honour, but I was prompted to refer to this because the indictment says that in the relevant time period, the accused - and I will quote from the English version - "worked in counter-intelligence." So I'm just asking whether Franko Simatovic was telling the truth with respect to his position. Did he tell Mr. Soldal this? Because Mr. Soldal says that he was insincere during the interview. But did he nevertheless provide some truthful information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Ask the question and then move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, in 1990 or 1991, the state security got their own intelligence branch. Before that, it had been a counter-intelligence organisation, and Simatovic became involved with the intelligence part of the DB.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what his formal position was with the Ministry of Internal Affairs at the time? He did hand over some documents to you. Did he tell you about his position?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: According to himself, he had quite a low-level position at that time. I don't remember the actual position he held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember. Very well. Thank you. Mr. Soldal, your view that Mr. Simatovic respected and respects the work of the International Criminal Tribunal, was it something that he did during the interview that led you in any way to believe that this was not in fact true?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: It's more the information he gave us than what he did during the interview. Most witnesses I interview claim they respect the work of the Tribunal and that they want to cooperate with us. The information they gave us can show that it's not actually the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal, please, if you could view these two things separately, how Mr. Simatovic treated you, his attitude in relation to the interview itself, how he behaved. This interview lasted a couple of days. Those were altogether 30 hours of conversation. On the one hand we have your general position on that, the way he confronted you, the way he provided information. This will later be subject to evaluation. Was it your conclusion that he talked to you voluntarily and that he was willing to cooperate to provide information? Let us just limit ourselves to that. Let us not now discuss the truthfulness of this information. But is it true that he was willing to provide information?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he did cooperate? Am I right in assuming that?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes. There were no problems during the interview, and I interviewed him six days altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal, you said that certain witnesses that you interviewed for the Milosevic case informed you that while the accused were still at large they were not willing to talk to you. Did those witnesses later testify in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Which time-frame are we talking about? Can you specify at which time you got in touch with those witnesses when they stated this to you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal, did those witnesses perhaps explain to you why their position was as it was? Because back then, there was no mention at all of Franko Simatovic being detained on any grounds whatsoever. What was this supposed to mean while these people were still at large? There were no signs back then, nothing to lead anyone to believe that Franko Simatovic would one day be detained.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No, but we very often met people that asked us why haven't you arrested Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic, and it's based on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you perhaps specify who these people are. Not information on these people, of course, but in relation to which circumstances they're supposed to testify and in which case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are people that the Prosecution will be filing motion for disclosure of their identity. I'm not sure of the relevance of their actual names at this juncture, but I would want to be heard extensively if Mr. Jovanovic feels it's that important to inquire about the identity of these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I believe there's been a misunderstanding. That's precisely what I'm saying. I do not need these people's identity. We can't have these statements disclosed now because, to begin with, these people have never testified. What I want to know is whether Mr. Soldal can specify who these witnesses were that refused to testify in the Milosevic case, requesting that Franko Simatovic be brought in before they do anything. Who were these people who requested that Franko Simatovic be detained, and who asked questions about when he would be detained? Is there a report that he sent to the OTP in relation to this issue? Is there any paper trail?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you answer that? We don't want the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is witnesses I interviewed during -- or tried to interview, more correctly, during the Milosevic investigation. And it's mostly members of the so-called Red Berets or other paramilitary units. And many of them asked if we were going to arrest Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you inform the OTP about this? Was there a report that was drafted on your part about this? I assume that before you approach a witness, you gather all the information that you can on that witness, and then you must produce something in return, following your contact with these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: If the witness interviews we are supposed to do in the field don't take place, we write a short report about the witness in the mission report we have to submit when we are back from mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do that in relation to the witnesses we are talking about now?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: The witnesses that refused to testify?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: It must have been done for several witnesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically these witnesses who referred to Mr. Simatovic? Did you enter that bit of information in your report?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: This happened with a lot of witnesses, and what kind of information I entered for each witness, I do not remember today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, to sum it up: You can't be sure that you actually wrote a report for the OTP in which you stated such-and-such witness refuses to talk to us, requesting that Franko Simatovic first be placed into custody.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: I have submitted reports about witnesses that don't want to be interviewed because of the two accused, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be more specific, please. Did you actually write this in your report, the specific reason?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: I know I have written reports about it, yes. For how many or for whom of them, I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal, what he's asking you is whether in your reports you specified that the witnesses told you that they were concerned about the two accused being at large. He's asking whether you specifically mentioned that in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have mentioned that in reports, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you perhaps show us these reports?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: I don't have them. I have to search through the system on my reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Soldal. In relation to witness B 190, during your interview of witness 190, you decided to view this witness as a suspect following information that he disclosed to you. He provided information on Croatia, as you said, refusing to provide information on Bosnia, because of the accused Simatovic and the alleged involved 9as interpreted] of this witness in a DB unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he talk about what happened in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that Franko Simatovic stands accused also of crimes committed in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: According to this witness, the reason why he was willing to talk about Croatia was that he belonged to another unit during that time-frame.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal, what is the procedure when a statement is taken from a suspect? What is the specific value of what a suspect tells you before or during the interview, the recorded interview, in view of Rule 42, of course?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: The procedure is that we always interview the suspect by using video or audio equipment. We read their rights. We don't discuss any facts related to the investigation outside the time. And the value is for the lawyers to review.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, what you talked about to witness 190 is essential, after all. It's about his involvement in the war in Bosnia. Do you believe that witness 190, by virtue of the fact that he asked you to stop the recording, wanted to avoid disclosing that particular information? Within his rights as a suspect, he refused to incriminate himself, and that's why he requested that the recording itself be stopped.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: According to the witness, that wasn't the reason. He was afraid because he belonged to the so-called Red Berets during the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that his statement to the effect that he was a member of the Red Berets during the conflict in Bosnia is something that incriminates him?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: It doesn't necessarily have to incriminate him, that he was a member of that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he certainly did not want to make this information public, did he?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 190, was he informed, or rather, did you inform him that today you would be speaking about his rights under Rule 42 and how he refused to talk about this?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal, paragraph 7 of your statement in relation to witness B073, is this your comment on what happened?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, this was a public testimony, if I'm not mistaken, wasn't it? There is a transcript on the website of this Tribunal. Therefore, the public has access to what happened. You saw it fit to comment on what happened, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes. I followed it on TV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, this only represents your own opinion and not necessarily shared by others, does it. As to the nature of these events, that's your opinion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Knoops:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal, if I understand your statement correctly, you actually refer with respect to specific the situation of Mr. Stanisic to one occurrence, which you elaborate on in paragraph 6 of your affidavit, a so-called sensitive source, indicating that there was some kind of a meeting at the house of Mr. Stanisic. Is that correct? So this is -- considering your statement, the only concrete incident you describe about Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honour, I believe that this next line of questioning may compromise the identity of that witness. Could I ask the Court to inquire from Mr. Soldal if he does believe that it will. And if it will, I'd asked that it occur in private session. Because of how events occurred in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Soldal, is there some matter that should be taken in private session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think let us hear the question. Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Defence will not try to find out the identity of the source, Your Honour, so can offer comfort to the Prosecution on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: First of all -- so I understand your answer, you say this is the only concrete incident I described about the potential involvement of Mr. Stanisic. I just -- I understood your question as affirming.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes, in this affidavit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this affidavit, right.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: And of course when witnesses are telling, you have -- I mentioned witness 174, 235. That is also related to DBS or state security as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But I'm speaking now on your affidavit on the 6th of May. Mr. Soldal, first of all, the information you obtained was from a person. Was the person himself present during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You describe that the way of conduct seemed to you as Mr. Stanisic wanted to screen the interviews we had with them. First of all, did you inquire about the nature of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to verify the nature of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: There were no way I could get that verified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you approach the two persons you mentioned as the two former members? Did you approach these persons as to the content of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in any way, in any other way, verify your impression that it seemed to you that Mr. Stanisic wanted to screen these interviews?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: I reviewed the statement of these two witnesses, and I also compared them with the statements of the two accused, and I could see similarities in the story they gave us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you deduced from some similarities your observation or your suggestion that conversation was apparently meant, in your view, to screen persons.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you any other arguments to substantiate your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No. And as I wrote in the affidavit, the dates for this meeting fall together with the dates for the interview. I think I wrote that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But you mentioned that as an argument to corroborate the time and the place. But I mean the contents of the meeting, apparently at the place of Mr. Stanisic, was that in any other way verified by you or only by comparing the statements?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Only by --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Comparison of the statements?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My second question to you, Mr. Soldal, is: You refer to potential witnesses who refused to be interviewed because they feared their own safety or the safety of their families at paragraph 3. And you also refer to the argument that, I quote: "Real power in the country was held by Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic." Did you in any way verify at what time Mr. Stanisic was dismissed from service?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: 1997 sometime, I think, or 1996. I don't have the exact time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the interviews you refer to, were they undertaken after the period you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yeah. A long time after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So actually, at the time of the interviews, Mr. Stanisic was not actually head of the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: He was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Still, these people you refer to apparently told you that the real power in the country remained -- was held by Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that for you a credible argument, considering the fact that, according to your statement, Mr. Stanisic was already for some years not in power of the DB?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: It's very difficult to tell whether -- anything credible or not. First of all, I'm not a political analyst. And secondly, there have been many governments down there. There have been a lot of problems with the different governments. So who is in power at any time has been difficult to say, at least for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Mr. Soldal, you agree on first sight that this is not quite logical that people allegedly saying that somebody is in power of a whole country, a whole state, while that person merely was during his service the civilian head of a security service and already left the service for years?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: None of them held any de jure power at that time in Serbia or Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in any way in the position to verify that suggestion made by these witnesses?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a last question for you, Mr. Soldal. Did you ever receive any concrete evidence that Mr. Stanisic himself tried to influence any witness, concrete evidence that he himself tried to influence a witness?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Soldal, that is your evidence and you may go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the programme that was issued on Friday, the order for the work today, we had scheduled a Status Conference, and we consider it appropriate to carry out that conference now in relation to the accused Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I quite agree. Before this hearing, talking to the Prosecution, I accepted the proposal suggested by Mr. Groome, and that is that he would suggest that we have a Status Conference. But I will be guided by your instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a Status Conference, taking this opportunity. But if there's any issues to raise at this moment, the Chamber would like to hear from the parties now. --- Motion Hearing adjourned for Simatovic Status Conference]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, we are coming to the close of your case, the hearing in respect of the accused Simatovic. Do you have any closing remarks to make, on the provisional release, of course?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, very briefly. With respect to the two witnesses heard and the information they provided us, first of all, we were able to see for ourselves that these were investigators who did not work alone. In the process of investigation, there are tasks performed by their colleagues and we had occasion to hear these witnesses saying that they are not fully informed as to what their colleagues had done. This is a system of work which is functioning perfectly, probably, with respect to the collection of information; but this supports what the Defence of the accused has been claiming, and that is only once all the relevant information have been collected and analysed, together with Defence evidence, can you, Your Honours, determine the facts beyond any reasonable doubt and proclaim someone guilty. So I feel that it is not up to the investigators of the OTP to pass such opinions. Mr. O'Donnell, in his statement, which we received this morning, said something that is common knowledge, that is, who is accused and who is not by this Tribunal, for one reason or another. But I think we were given a clear explanation by the minister of justice, Mr. Stojkovic, that in some situations there may be differences from one situation to another. Mr. Soldal, on the other hand, was very clear in saying that Mr. Simatovic was more than willing to receive the investigators in his own apartment and to cooperate with them. He was interviewed as a suspect. He didn't take the oath. He was defending himself. Now, when the information he provided were accurate, it is up to you to establish [as interpreted]. I think up to this point in time, we cannot rely on the information of the Prosecution as to what is truthful and what is not. It is quite clear that there are some facts that are contradictory, even facts in the possession of the Prosecution, and it is only with time and with the assistance of the Defence will all this be cleared up. And before all that is done, I think we cannot find facts to be established. I think the Prosecution is trying to prejudge certain things. If the accused were not to be provisionally released, this would be a way of justifying their position, and I think that is not acceptable. And I feel that the testimony of the two witnesses confirms the position of the Defence, that the accused fully cooperated. There was no evidence of any kind of threat by Mr. Franko Simatovic. Mr. Soldal mentioned some witnesses who allegedly refused to testify, but there was no evidence that he could provide. He can't remember who those witnesses are, how many witnesses, et cetera. Therefore, it is my submission that Franko Simatovic, on the basis of what has been said by these two witnesses, have not managed to convince the Trial Chamber that Franko Simatovic will influence witnesses, victims, or any third persons, and that the submissions of the Defence have been corroborated. Also, regarding Mr. Soldal, who watched trial by TV, that is not relevant. And in the response of the Prosecution does not clearly identify the status of that transcript. Any transcript, any statement by that witness, has not been produced on the basis of which we might be able to investigate that event, and I think this is an allegation by the Prosecution which the Chamber should not rely on. Therefore, I stand by the proposal that I made in my opening statement. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Any reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Before I begin, I think I have about five to ten minutes of remarks. Does time permit me to begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it will be in the interest of expediting the proceedings if you proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, in October of 2002, the Appeals Chamber issued a decision denying the provisional release, the applications of Nikola Sainovic and Dragoljub Ojdanic. In paragraph 6, the judgement of the Appeals Chambers set out nine factors which it said it expected the Trial Chamber to consider in that case, and found that the Trial Chamber had committed an error of law in not addressing them. Recognising that the facts of each case may be somewhat different, will nonetheless construct my remarks around the nine factors set out by the Appeals Chamber. The first two are seriousness of the charges and likelihood of long sentences. I will deal with those together. They are firstly -- I'm sorry. As the Trial Chamber in the Brdjanin case stated, "It is a matter of common experience that the more serious the charge the greater the likely sentence if convicted and the greater reasons for not appearing at trial." I will not summarise the indictment charges or the underlying crimes. As has been pointed out by a number of Trial Chambers considering provisional release, the cases heard in this building are by mandate and by their very nature cases of a very grave nature. I think it is useful for the Chamber to consider that on the spectrum of cases running from the very grave to the even graver still, this case falls somewhere in the vicinity of one of the gravest indictments brought before a Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not only by the serious and large numbers of victims by perpetrators it is alleged these men employed in their criminal plan, men such as Arkan, Legija, Lugar, and Debeli. It is the Prosecution's view that both of these men were centrally placed and responsible for many of the crimes that were perpetrated in Croatia and Bosnia, that the machinery and mechanisms that they personally built and supplied under the patronage and direction of Mr. Milosevic played a critical and criminal law in the excesses of the Yugoslav conflict. I am sufficiently familiar with the evidence and victims in this case that I am reasonably sure at the conclusion of a trial I would be arguing to the Chamber that if it finds the Prosecution has proven this indictment beyond reasonable doubt, I would be arguing that a maximum sentence should be imposed. In summary, there are few indictments more serious than the one before the Chamber, on indictment which, if the Prosecution meets its burden, will likely result in a significant sentence. With respect to the circumstances under which they came into custody, this would be the third factor in the Sainovic Appeals Chamber judgement. Common sense dictates that if an accused surrendered voluntarily, once more he is likely to do so in the future, and this factor admittedly has always been an important one. I do recognise and report to the Chamber that Mr. Simatovic did tell the investigators who were interviewing him that should he be indicted, he requested that he be informed so he could turn himself in voluntarily. What transpired after his arrest in Serbia did not give him the opportunity to demonstrate that intention. So we have no basis of knowing whether or not he would have in fact voluntarily surrendered. But I do recognise that he did explicitly state that to the investigators who spoke with him. The fourth factor: Guarantees of the relevant governments. One of the important evaluations a Trial Chamber must engage itself in when presented with an application for provisional release is the reliability of any guarantees presented. The Appeals Chamber in the 8th of October, 2002 decision, in the case of the Prosecutor versus Mrksic, defined the test as follows, in paragraph 9: "The reliability of a guarantee given by the relevant authority must be determined in relation to the circumstances which arise in the particular case. The issue in each particular case is what would occur if the relevant authority were obliged, under its guarantee, to arrest the accused person seeking provisional release in that case." The Appeals Chamber went on to illustrate this point, citing an example of two hypothetical accused, one which had a bona fide intention to appear for trial, and the other which was in possession of highly important and sensitive information. And the Appeals Chamber said the following: "Accused B may have been a high-level government official at the time he is alleged to have committed the crimes charged; and he may have since then lost political influence but yet possesses very valuable information which he could disclose to the Tribunal if minded to cooperate, should he be kept in custody. There would be a substantial disincentive for that authority to enforce its guarantee to arrest that particular accused if he did not comply with the conditions of his provisional release." Based upon the indictment and based upon the evidence that the Chamber has heard here today, I would submit that Mr. Simatovic would very well fit into the category of an accused B, a high-level person no longer in power, with very valuable information. I also point out with respect to reliability of the guarantee, President Meron's letter of last week in which he stated in one of the latter paragraph of that letter quoting: "I view the report of the Prosecutor as indicating extremely serious failures on the part of Serbia and Montenegro, and the Prosecutor has satisfied me that Serbia and Montenegro is failing to comply with its obligations under Article 29 of the Statute and Rule 39 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I do not question the sincerity of Minister Stojkovic in his testimony today when he said he was willing to abide by the obligation towards the Tribunal. It is the Prosecution's position, though, that the most reliable indication of whether or not these guarantees will be adhered to, if necessary, is the past track record. And as the Chamber has heard from Mr. O'Donnell -- I believe the number he gave was 16 indictees for whom information in possession of the Prosecution, that these people were in Serbia and Montenegro of -- when that information was passed on, there were no tangible results as a result of passing on that information. The fifth factor in the Sainovic Appeals Chamber judgement was the level of position held by the accused in relation to the weight accorded the guarantee. I believe I've covered that. The sixth factor was the law on cooperation. I think it's very important to note Minister Stojkovic's testimony regarding there is no council for cooperation in effect at present. There is no body to regulate cooperation. The seventh is the personal guarantees provided by the accused. Again, I would ask the Chamber to take them in light of my comments with respect to the first two factors. The eighth factor is the likelihood that relevant authorities will rearrest the accused if he refuses to surrender. Throughout the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, one repeating theme or recurring theme is that this Tribunal lacks the capacity to go out and make arrests itself and it is very dependent upon the countries where the accused are living to do that. One of the important factors that I think the Chamber should consider - and I suggest this to distinguish the cases of Plavsic and Strugar and Jokic - is that if these men, or if Mr. Simatovic, for today's purposes, was not to adhere to his obligation to return, who is it who would be sent out to arrest him? It would be people from the Ministry of the Interior, the very organisation where it is alleged that he held a very high and very influential position. With respect to passport, in Serbia and Montenegro, it's the Ministry of the Interior that regulates those passports. Again, Mr. Simatovic had a very important position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, that was in a different era, when he held the high position in the DB.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I recognise that, Your Honour. And tomorrow when I make my comments with respect to Mr. Stanisic, I will point out that one of the things he said to the Doctor, Mr. Offermans, was Mr. Stanisic admitted that he still has very important contacts in among his old contacts who are from the positions he held. I would ask the Court -- suggest to the Court although Mr. Simatovic has not made a similar admission, is also still -- quite possible that Mr. Simatovic would have a considerable amount of influence. And even though he does not hold the same position, I think it's safe to say that many of the people who are his subordinates who were there when he did hold that position still are in the ministry today and still would be subject to some of the influence of Mr. Simatovic. I propose to the Court that it would be a very difficult thing for some of those people to have to go out and arrest him if that became necessary. With respect to the agreement or their willingness to be interviewed, I will rely on the testimony and the affidavits of the two investigators, in particular with respect to Mr. Simatovic, that of Mr. Soldal, and would suggest to the Court that their eagerness to cooperate and to give statements is equally consistent with somebody who is aware that they are being investigated and gives a self-serving statement as it is with somebody who is honestly trying to report their truthful account of events as they recall them. In fact, I would suggest that given the testimony we've heard today, that the first proposition is the more likely one. And I would conclude my remarks with respect to Mr. Simatovic there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That concludes the hearing in respect of the accused Simatovic. We adjourn, and we'll resume tomorrow. Before we break, a comment on the availability of witnesses. Senior Legal Officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand -- I think this concerns Mr. Knoops - that the minister of health, the professor, is not available; Dr. Tarabar is available; Dr. Offermans is not available. And for the Prosecution, Dr. Smalc is available, is she?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. She arrives today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And we are to discuss a suitable date for Dr. Boomgaard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll do that later. Are you aware of that -- were you aware of that position?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we weren't. No. But I've just confirmed that we also for the sake of time, we will waive the hearing of the minister of health. But we do like to hear Dr. Offermans, and perhaps if you have a chance to schedule him on Thursday, we would try to contact him today. Whether he is available on Thursday. I'm sure he must have a possibility this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd like to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In relation to the minister of health before waiving him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. But we were just informed that he already left. He checked out. So I'm expecting to -- but we will check it and inform your Chamber about his exact location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's always good to carry out investigations of your own. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just going to say, in a slightly related manner, that my comments with respect to conducting an examination in the back, of course, are the same. We do now have the English translation of the Detention Unit medical records giving the most up-to-date diagnostic information about the accused Mr. Stanisic. I would have no objection to Mr. Knoops giving his experts a copy of these documents if they want to review the medical records of people who have done recent examination of Mr. Stanisic and have recorded their observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber had already made a ruling on that and we expect it to be respected. We are adjourned until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 11th day of May, 2004, at 3 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2 p.m.,
